p: Ahmad Khan, of the Sadozai lineage of the Abdali tribe, was the son of Muhammad Zaman Khan, who had served as governor of Herat, and a commander under Nader Shah. After Nader Shah's death in June 1747 a loya jirga, or grand council, met near Kandahar for nine days. The two chief contestants were Hajji Jamal Khan of the Mohammadzai and Ahmad Khan. A holy man, Mohammad Sabir Khan, spoke for Ahmad Khan, reputedly placed sheaves of wheat or barley in his turban and crowned him with the title Durr-i-Durran, Pearl of the Pearls, from which the tribe took the name Durrani.

Ahmad Shah took Qalati Ghilji and Ghazni from the Ghilji and Kabul and Peshawar from the Mughal governor Nasir Khan. In 1749 the Mughal emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur ceded Sindh and the Punjab to save his capital, and Ahmad Shah then took Mashhad from Shahrukh Afshar and subdued the peoples north of the Hindu Kush. He sacked Delhi in 1757. In 1762 his forces killed thousands of Sikhs in the Punjab, in what Sikhs call the Vaḍḍā Ghallūghārā, and destroyed the Golden Temple at Amritsar, yet the Sikhs rebuilt it and he never subdued them. He died east of Kandahar in 1772.

His son Timur Shah Durrani took the throne in November 1772 and made Kabul the capital. Timur's sons fought one another: Zaman Shah, who succeeded in 1793, was blinded and replaced by Mahmud Shah in 1801, and Shuja Shah ruled from 1803 to 1809. On 7 June 1809 Shuja signed with the British East India Company the first Afghan pact with a European power. By 1818 the Sadozai rulers held little more than Kabul and the land within 160 kilometres of it. Kashmir was lost to the Sikh Empire at the Battle of Shopian in 1819, and Ayub Shah was deposed in 1823.

The army was based on cavalry armed with flintlocks, who made hit-and-run attacks. Its core was 10,000 mounted ghulams, or slave-soldiers, carrying blunderbusses; a third of them were Qizilbash who had served Nader Shah. The bulk of the army was irregular Afghan tribal cavalry armed with lance and broadsword, and infantry played a very small part. Ahmad Shah balanced tribal alliances and hostilities, a balance his successors upset when they tried to rule without the other Durrani chiefs. The Barakzai under Dost Muhammad Khan later displaced the dynasty at Kabul, and the empire is regarded as the foundation of the modern Afghan state.

notes: The lead of the article says the Maratha Empire 'controlled eastern Afghanistan' in 1749; the body does not support it and I left it out.
The article counts 'eight' invasions of India in the lead and calls the 1762 crossing the 'sixth'; I gave no count.
The long 'Relations with China' section (embassy of 1763, Badakhshan 1768) was left out for room. The Timur Shah section of the saved article is empty.
'what Sikhs call the Vaḍḍā Ghallūghārā' is my framing of the article's name for the 1762 killings; the article says 'thousands'.
